case_study_insert.main_stem: Marlowe Hill Furniture (MHF) is a family partnership in the reclaimed furniture and eco-materials sector, employing a workforce of 26. Founded in 2013 by Callum Marlowe, the business makes reclaimed-timber furniture for interior designers and operates a hierarchical structure with democratic leadership. MHF plans to invest $540,000 in a reclaimed-timber workshop with low-VOC eco-finishes, financed by $220,000 of hire purchase on machinery and $320,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $156,000 a year, a variable cost of $9.00 a unit and a selling price of $16.50, and produces 60,000 units of furniture a year. MHF faces two problems: a shortage of skilled joiners and a rising rate of finish defects.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Operations and Quality Log — Q3 2025: The reclaimed-timber workshop produced 15,000 units last quarter at a defect rate of 2.9%, up from 1.7% a year ago as new joiners learned the eco-finishing line. Finish rework cost $0.60 per unit on average. Customer complaints rose from 16 to 29 per month. Average order lead time is 6.2 days. A survey of 380 interior designers found that 66% would pay up to $0.80 more for furniture made from reclaimed materials, and 53% check the source of timber before specifying it. A skills audit shows 9 of 26 staff lack on-the-job training in low-VOC spraying; off-the-job courses at the college cost $720 per employee.

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.00% to 4.75%, increasing the cost of the $220,000 hire-purchase agreement. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.4% from $12.90 to $13.60 per hour from April 2026, raising total wage bills. (3) Reclaimed timber and low-VOC finish input costs rose 10.6% year-on-year, while consumer spending on home furniture fell 1.4% over the same period.

questions.question_text: MHF plans to fund its reclaimed-timber workshop with retained profit rather than the $220,000 hire purchase. Explain two advantages for MHF of using the $320,000 retained profit instead of hire purchase.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Using $320,000 of retained profit avoids the regular hire-purchase instalments and interest charges on the $220,000 machinery agreement, protecting cash flow while the partnership already meets fixed costs of $156,000 a year. The money saved can be spent on tackling the 2.9% finish defect rate and the $0.60 per unit rework cost, or absorbed if reclaimed timber and low-VOC finish costs rise 10.6%, allowing MHF to hold its $16.50 selling price for interior designers.

Point 2: Retained profit gives no lender the right to repossess the new workshop machinery if orders slip, so Callum Marlowe and the other partners keep control of the $540,000 investment and the reclaimed furniture range. Hire purchase would tie the partners to fixed payments and security regardless of the shortage of skilled joiners or the 1.4% fall in furniture spending. Internal funds also preserve the partnership's borrowing capacity for later phases of the workshop and avoid committing future profits to finance charges at a time when contribution per unit is under pressure.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to MHF's cash flow, defects and partnership control.

questions.question_text: MHF is promoting its reclaimed-timber furniture to interior designers. Consider advertising in interior-design magazines, sponsoring a home-design exhibition, or an influencer-led social media campaign. Which should MHF choose? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Interior-design magazine advertising: A magazine placed in the titles read by specifiers can show high-quality photographs of MHF's reclaimed-timber pieces and explain the low-VOC finishes, reaching the 53% of surveyed designers who check timber sources. It is a respected medium that supports a premium $16.50 price. However, it is expensive for a 26-person partnership with a $540,000 workshop to fund, the readership is broader than MHF's buyer group, and print cannot demonstrate the reclaimed material's quality or respond quickly to the 1.4% fall in furniture spending.

Home-design exhibition sponsorship: A sponsored stand lets designers see and touch the furniture, ask about reclaimed sources and verify the low-VOC finishes, directly addressing the 53% who check timber origins. It also supports the 66% who would pay $0.80 more by making the craftsmanship visible. The drawbacks are the cost of a quality stand, reach limited to attendees, and the fact that a single exhibition cannot fill the orders required for 60,000 units a year.

Influencer-led social media campaign: Working with interiors influencers puts MHF's reclaimed pieces in front of the designers and homeowners who influence specifications, telling the reclaimed-source story in short video form. It is measurable, relatively cheap per contact and can highlight the $0.80 premium message. It depends on choosing credible influencers and needs sustained content, and it may not reach older designers who specify through trade channels.

Recommendation: MHF should choose the influencer-led social media campaign. It targets the 66% of the 380 designers who value reclaimed materials and the 53% who check sources at low cost, and it scales nationally in a way one exhibition cannot. The exhibition is rejected as too narrow and costly; magazines are rejected as expensive and untargeted. A small exhibition presence can later support the digital campaign.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited outline of the promotional options with minimal application to MHF.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of MHF with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of MHF with a well-justified recommendation explaining why magazines and the exhibition are rejected.

questions.question_text: MHF has a hierarchical structure with democratic leadership, but faces a shortage of skilled joiners and finish defects. Explain two benefits for MHF of this leadership approach in tackling those problems.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Democratic leadership within the hierarchy lets MHF's 26 staff put forward practical ideas on the low-VOC spraying line, so the joiners closest to the work can identify why the defect rate rose from 1.7% to 2.9% and suggest fixes. Their involvement raises job satisfaction and commitment, which helps retain the skilled joiners MHF lacks and protects the 60,000-unit output needed to justify the $540,000 workshop.

Point 2: Consulting the team over working methods spreads ownership of quality, so the 9 staff without on-the-job training in low-VOC spraying can learn from experienced colleagues and reduce the $0.60 per unit rework cost. Better involvement also improves the 6.2-day lead time and helps answer the complaints that rose from 16 to 29 per month, strengthening the reputation for reclaimed furniture that supports the $16.50 price and the 53% of designers who check timber sources.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to MHF's skills shortage, defects and output.

questions.question_text: MHF must train 9 of its 26 staff in low-VOC spraying. Consider on-the-job training in the workshop or off-the-job courses at the college at $720 per employee. Which should MHF choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Coaching on MHF's own finishing line teaches the 9 trainees the exact spraying routines behind the reclaimed-timber furniture, costs no course fee, and keeps them producing while they learn, which protects the 15,000 units made last quarter. Experienced joiners can demonstrate how to cut the 2.9% defect rate and the $0.60 per unit rework cost. The drawbacks are that the trainers lose time, bad habits may spread, and there is no external certificate, which may matter to the 53% of designers who check timber sources and want assurance on low-VOC finishes.

Off-the-job training: The college course at $720 per employee costs $6,480 for all 9 staff (9 × $720), small against the $540,000 workshop, and gives structured teaching plus a recognised certificate that supports MHF's eco-finish claims. However, 9 of 26 staff are away from the workshop, slowing the 6.2-day lead time, and the course may not cover MHF's exact spraying equipment, so on-site follow-up would still be needed.

Decision: MHF should choose on-the-job training as the main method, with a short college module for certification. It is cheaper, specific to the low-VOC line and avoids output loss while the shortage of skilled joiners is acute; full off-the-job training alone is rejected because removing 9 staff and spending $6,480 would disrupt the 60,000-unit plan and still leave machine-specific habits to be learned on site.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to MHF.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of one or both training methods in the context of MHF.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both training methods in the context of MHF with a well-justified decision covering cost, disruption and finishing relevance.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how MHF's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $156,000 ÷ ($16.50 − $9.00) = $156,000 ÷ $7.50 = 20,800 units. Answer: break-even output is 20,800 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $16.50 − $9.00 = $7.50. Answer: contribution per unit is $7.50.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways MHF's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Break-even of 20,800 units against output of 60,000 units gives a margin of safety of 39,200 units (60,000 − 20,800), showing how far furniture demand could fall before the reclaimed-timber workshop stops covering its $156,000 fixed costs.
2. Contribution of $7.50 a unit lets managers test the $0.80 premium: if designers accept it, contribution would rise toward $8.30; if not, the partnership still needs 20,800 units to break even, informing price negotiations.
3. The figures set the sales volume required to meet the $220,000 hire-purchase payments and justify the $540,000 investment, guiding how much reclaimed timber to source.
4. Unit cost data ($156,000 ÷ 60,000 units + $9.00 = $11.60 a unit) enables quarterly benchmarking, exposing the 2.9% defect rate and $0.60 rework cost so managers can act on the 10.6% rise in timber and finish prices.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 20,800 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $7.50 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety of 39,200 units against 60,000-unit output; testing the $0.80 premium against $156,000 fixed costs; hire-purchase and $540,000 volume planning; and unit-cost benchmarking at $11.60 to cut rework.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method and 1 mark for the accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate MHF's financial performance by calculating the gross profit margin, profit margin and ROCE for 2024 and 2025. Has performance improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 40.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 45.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 12.0%
Profit Margin 2025 = 15.0%
ROCE 2024 = 12.0%
ROCE 2025 = 15.0%

Detailed workings: 2024 gross profit of $280,000 on revenue of $700,000 gives 280 ÷ 700 = 0.400; 2025 gross profit of $360,000 on $800,000 gives 360 ÷ 800 = 0.450. Operating profit of $84,000 ÷ $700,000 = 0.120 and $120,000 ÷ $800,000 = 0.150. Returns on capital employed of $700,000 and $800,000 are 84 ÷ 700 = 0.120 and 120 ÷ 800 = 0.150.

Evaluation: Each measure is higher. The 40.0% to 45.0% rise in the first margin reflects revenue growing by $100,000 while cost of sales rose by only $20,000, so MHF earned more from reclaimed furniture without a matching rise in material spending. The 12.0% to 15.0% rise in operating profitability shows the $156,000 fixed costs were covered more effectively, and the 12.0% to 15.0% return on capital shows the growing asset base is working harder. Offsetting this, interest payable rose from $16,000 to $21,000 as the $220,000 hire-purchase commitment grew, and the 10.6% rise in reclaimed timber and low-VOC finish costs may erode the cost-of-sales gain next year. The 2.9% defect rate and $0.60 rework also drag on efficiency.

Conclusion: MHF's performance has improved. Higher revenue, a much smaller rise in cost of sales and stronger operating profit lift both margins and the return on capital. The main risks are rising finance charges and input inflation, which the partners should monitor, but on the 2024–2025 evidence the improvement is real and well founded.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the three profitability measures for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of revenue, cost of sales, capital employed and interest movements and a justified conclusion on whether performance improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for MHF of using reclaimed timber and low-VOC eco-finishes in its furniture.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Reclaimed timber and low-VOC finishes match the survey result that 66% of the 380 interior designers questioned would pay up to $0.80 more, protecting the $7.50 contribution per unit even though reclaimed timber and finish costs have risen 10.6%. The same story appeals to the 53% who check timber sources, supporting the $540,000 workshop and the 60,000-unit output sold at the $16.50 price.

Disadvantage: Reclaimed timber varies in grade and supply, which can lift the 2.9% defect rate and the $0.60 per unit rework cost as joiners adapt, while low-VOC finishes may cost more than standard coatings and push up the $9.00 variable cost. Unless the full $0.80 premium is won across customers, MHF's margins will be squeezed at a time when the shortage of skilled joiners and the 1.4% fall in furniture spending already make the workshop's first year uncertain.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to MHF's survey data, costs and finish quality.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 4.75%, the 5.4% minimum wage increase and the 10.6% rise in reclaimed timber and low-VOC finish costs will affect MHF. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.00% to 4.75%): If the $220,000 hire-purchase agreement is linked to the base rate, a 0.75 percentage point increase adds 0.0075 × $220,000 = $1,650 a year. That is small compared with fixed costs of $156,000, and the $320,000 retained profit used for the workshop means MHF has limited rate-sensitive debt. The wider concern is that dearer credit could deter interior-design customers in a market where furniture spending already fell 1.4%.

Minimum wage increase (5.4%, to $13.60 an hour): MHF employs a workforce of 26, including joiners and finishing staff, so wage costs will rise and cannot be avoided. The insert gives no hours worked and no individual pay, so a total wage bill cannot be calculated honestly. The defensible test is productivity: 60,000 units ÷ 26 staff ≈ 2,308 units per employee, so the rise is affordable only if the new workshop maintains that output and the 2.9% defect rate is brought under control; otherwise unit labour cost erodes the $7.50 contribution.

Timber and finish costs (10.6%): These are core inputs into reclaimed furniture. Because the $9.00 variable cost is not decomposed, only a labelled bound can be shown: if all of it rose 10.6%, that adds 0.106 × $9.00 = $0.95 per unit (rounded); across 60,000 units that is $57,000 a year (60,000 × $0.95). Even a partial rise would cut contribution from $7.50 toward about $6.55, and the $0.80 premium available to 66% of designers offsets only part of it.

Conclusion: The 10.6% rise in reclaimed timber and low-VOC finish costs will have the greatest impact. It hits every unit, directly reduces the contribution that services the hire purchase and underpins the $540,000 workshop, and cannot be removed by refinancing. The interest effect is small and limited at $1,650, while the wage effect depends on hours not stated and can be offset by productivity, so both are secondary.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external changes with limited application to MHF.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on MHF's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of MHF with a well-justified judgment that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
